analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $6.50 and automatically adjusts it with inflation each year.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage to $6.50 and index it to inflation was introduced by one Independent with a single Democratic cosponsor and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.50 an hour starting after December 30, 1999 [S2][S3]. It would also have tied the minimum wage to the cost of living, adjusting it every year the same way Social Security benefits are adjusted, so Congress would no longer have to pass a new law each time prices rise [S2][S3]. The bill was sent to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning the federal minimum wage of $5.15 an hour would see their pay rise to $6.50 — about a 26% increase — and then keep rising automatically with inflation, instead of waiting years for Congress to act [S2][S3]. Roughly the same group benefits from the indexing: in the 1990s Congress had let the minimum wage sit for years before raising it, and automatic adjustment would end that cycle.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $6.50 an hour beginning after December 30, 1999 [S2][S3].
Automatically adjusts the minimum wage each year by the same cost-of-living formula used for Social Security benefits, so the wage keeps pace with prices without new legislation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay the minimum wage — concentrated in restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service businesses — would bear the higher payroll. Some of that cost could reach consumers through prices, and some workers could face reduced hours or hiring in the industries most affected.

drawbacks.text: The increase from $5.15 to $6.50 is roughly 26% in one step, and employers of minimum-wage workers would bear it directly; small businesses in low-wage sectors argued then, as now, that sharp increases force price hikes, reduced hours, or slower hiring.

Automatic annual indexing removes the legislative pause that lets wages and local conditions adjust before the next increase — a feature some economists support and others criticize as inflexible in a downturn.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to low-wage workers is direct and substantial: a 26% raise plus a permanent end to the decade-long gaps between federal minimum-wage increases. The cost falls on businesses that employ minimum-wage workers, spread through prices and margins. The main design question is the one-step size of the increase and the rigidity of automatic indexing, but the core trade-off — worker pay versus employer labor costs — is straightforward.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House education committee and then a subcommittee, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, an Independent, introduced the bill on February 8, 1999 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day [S1][S5].
On February 26, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where no further action was recorded [S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, a Democrat, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 without the bill ever leaving committee [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers are better off, because the wage stayed at $5.15 with no cost-of-living adjustments. Workers who would have received the raise and the automatic annual increases gained nothing from the bill's death.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was an Independent and the only cosponsor was one Democrat; no Republican signed on, and neither party ever brought the bill to a vote, so no roll-call record shows where members stood.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (restaurants, retail, and other service businesses)
industries.note: The bill would have raised the wage floor these businesses pay by roughly 26% and then raised it every year with inflation. Because their gain from keeping the wage at $5.15 came directly out of workers' pay, their interest in this bill ran against the people it would help.
